claims.text: A multiscale model that separately simulates phonon and electronic transport in HfNbTaTiZr will predict total thermal conductivity with less than 20% error.
Separating phonon-mediated and electron-mediated thermal transport will outperform analytical approaches that conflate the two contributions.
The modeled initial material is defect-free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr.
The modeled material may contain a controlled addition of approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed approach combines DFT-derived elastic and force-constant data for phonon transport with independent electronic-structure calculations.
The model is intended to apply from approximately 100 K to 1200 K.
DFT-derived atomic structure determines the phonon dispersion and electronic band structure used by the model.
Atomic-scale structure mediates carrier scattering and heat-transport dynamics.
Temperature-dependent anharmonic force constants can capture phonon scattering accurately.
Electronic band-structure information can determine the electronic thermal-conduction behavior.
Independent treatment of phonon and electronic channels avoids errors associated with averaged parameters such as Debye temperature.
For HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, the model will reproduce total thermal conductivity values of approximately 10–17 W/(m K) from 300 K to 1200 K.
The model will reproduce comparable lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions below 200 K.
The model will reduce predictive error by approximately 20%–30% relative to existing unified analytical approaches.
Existing analytical and simulation approaches combine lattice and electronic effects through averaged parameters.
Existing approaches have errors above 30% in some temperature regimes.
The model may become unreliable below 100 K because quantum effects dominate.
The model may become unreliable above 1200 K because microstructural degradation or defect generation alters transport.
Uncertain electron-phonon coupling strengths and additional defects or impurities may reduce model accuracy.
Combined transport measurements can separately resolve lattice and electronic contributions sufficiently to test the model.
